passage:
Emeka's phone rang during dinner in their Lagos flat. A calm, official voice: 'This is your mother's bank. Her account has been flagged. Don't tell her yet, it will alarm her. We need you to buy gift cards to secure the funds, right now, and read me the codes.'
Emeka's heart thudded. Then he remembered what Wei had shown him in computer class: a list of three things real banks never do. Ask for secrecy. Demand payment immediately. Ask for gift cards.
This call had done all three.
'I'll call the bank back on the official number,' he said.
'There's no time, you'll be responsible if—'
He hung up. His hands were shaking a little. He went to the kitchen, told his mother everything, and they found the number printed on the back of her bank card. The real bank said: no problem with the account. Please report the call.

qa.q: Where did Emeka and his mother find the bank's official number?
qa.a: They found it printed on the back of her bank card.

qa.q: How did Emeka feel during the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt scared under pressure, with his heart thudding and hands shaking, but stayed clear-headed enough to check.

qa.q: Why was Emeka's rule of pausing and calling the official number so effective?
qa.a: Real banks never ask for secrecy, instant payment or gift cards, so pausing to check through an official number exposed the scam straight away.

qa.q: How might Emeka's mother feel after hearing what happened?
qa.a: She is likely relieved and proud that Emeka didn't keep it secret and came straight to her.

grounding: It shows a teen recognising secrecy, urgency and gift-card demands as scam signs, pausing and checking through an official number with a parent.

passage:
The school's computer lab was hot, and half the Class 10 students were fanning themselves with notebooks when Rukmini ma'am put up a message on the projector.
'Your parcel is held at customs. Pay a small fee within 30 minutes or it will be returned. Do not share this link.'
'What's wrong with it?' she asked.
Kamal put up his hand. 'Hurry. Secret. Pay by link.'
'Exactly. Real couriers, banks and police don't ask you to keep things secret or pay instantly. So what's our rule?'
The class said it together, half-laughing: 'Pause. Check the official number. Tell an adult.'
Two weeks later Kamal got almost the same message on his own phone, about a parcel he had actually ordered. For a second his thumb hovered over the link. Then he stopped, found the courier's number on its real website with his father, and called. No fee. No held parcel.
He deleted the message and reported it.

qa.q: How long did the fake message give to pay the fee?
qa.a: It said to pay within 30 minutes.

qa.q: What was Kamal thinking when his thumb hovered over the link?
qa.a: He felt unsure for a second because he really had ordered a parcel, but then remembered the rule and stopped.

qa.q: What made the class rule useful in a real moment?
qa.a: A short rule of pause, check the official number and tell an adult was easy to remember under pressure and worked against the scam.

qa.q: How might Rukmini ma'am feel if she heard what Kamal did?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased that the lesson worked outside the classroom.

grounding: It shows a teen learning that real institutions never demand secrecy or instant payment, then pausing and checking through an official number.

passage:
Hi Sonali didi,
You'll be proud of me. Yesterday I got a message that said it was from the bank: "Your account will be blocked today. Share the OTP and pay a fee through gift cards to unblock. Keep this confidential." It had the bank's logo and everything. My heart was going fast, because it's the account Papa opened for my scholarship.
Then I remembered what you said at Diwali: real banks never ask for OTPs, secrecy or gift cards, and never rush you. Pause first.
So I didn't reply. I showed Papa. We turned the bank card over and called the number printed on the back, not the one in the message. The bank person said, "This is a scam, please don't share anything." Papa reported the message the same evening.
Papa said I handled it better than he would have. I'm still a bit shaky, honestly. But mostly happy.
Naveen

qa.q: Which number did Naveen and Papa call?
qa.a: The number printed on the back of the bank card.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Naveen felt scared and rushed, heart going fast because it was the scholarship account.

qa.q: What rule helped Naveen, and why does it work?
qa.a: Pause and check through the official number; scams depend on urgency and secrecy, which a pause and a real call break.

qa.q: How might Sonali didi feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sonali would likely feel proud and relieved that the Diwali advice worked when it mattered.

grounding: A teen recognises that a real bank never demands secrecy, instant payment or gift cards, pauses, and checks through the official number.

passage:
Sudha, okay, so you know I've been playing that football game for months. Last week I got a message: "Congratulations, you've won a rare player pack! Buy two gift cards within ten minutes to claim, and don't tell anyone or it gets cancelled." A timer was ticking on the screen. My hands were literally sweating. I'd wanted that pack forever.
But three things felt off. Real companies don't want gift cards. They don't give you ten minutes. And why would a prize need to be secret?
So I closed it. Didn't click anything. I told my mum, and we found the game company's official support page ourselves, not through the link. They said they never send messages like that. Mum and I reported it together.
The silly part? I still wanted the pack. But I'd rather lose a fake prize than real money. Akash's rule: if it's urgent and secret, it's fake.

qa.q: How long did the message give Akash to claim the prize?
qa.a: Within ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Akash feel while the timer was ticking?
qa.a: Akash felt tempted and anxious, hands sweating, because it was a prize wanted for a long time.

qa.q: What made Akash's response effective?
qa.a: Pausing, spotting the gift cards, rush and secrecy, telling Mum, and checking the official support page directly.

qa.q: How might Sudha react hearing this story?
qa.a: Sudha might feel impressed and a bit relieved, and more alert to similar prize messages.

grounding: A teen spots that a prize demanding gift cards, speed and secrecy is fake, pauses, tells a parent and checks the official page.

passage:
I was doing homework at the dining table when Simran's phone rang, and she put it on speaker by mistake. A man said he was from the cyber police and that a parcel in her name contained illegal items. "You must pay a fine now or we come to your house. Do not tell your parents. This is confidential."
Simran's face went white. I thought she'd burst into tears. But she took a slow breath and said, "I'm fourteen. I'll call you back after checking." The man began shouting. She hung up.
Then she walked straight to the kitchen and told our mother. Jahnavi didn't panic. She found the official cyber-crime helpline number on the government website, called it, and reported the caller's number while Simran sat beside her.
I don't know exactly what Simran was feeling. Her hands were shaking. But she did everything right.

qa.q: Who did the caller claim to be?
qa.a: From the cyber police.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when the caller demanded secrecy?
qa.a: She was likely terrified, face white and hands shaking, yet calm enough to pause.

qa.q: Which of Simran's actions protected her, and why?
qa.a: Hanging up and telling her mother at once; real police do not demand secret, instant fines, and an adult could check the official helpline.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel as Simran tells her?
qa.a: Jahnavi is probably alarmed but calm and proud, glad her daughter came straight to her.

grounding: A sibling watches a teen refuse a fake police call demanding secrecy and payment, tell a parent, and check through the official helpline.

passage:
Monday: in the school's cyber-safety talk, the speaker wrote three lines on the board: "Real banks don't ask for secrecy. Real officers don't want gift cards. Real deadlines don't expire in ten minutes." Eshaan copied them into the back of his maths notebook, mostly because Siddharth dared him to.
Thursday: at 4 pm, Eshaan's phone buzzed. "Your school fee account will be BLOCKED. Pay the pending amount by gift card within 30 minutes. Do not tell anyone, as this is confidential." His heart jumped. Papa had paid the fees late once before. Then he remembered the back of his notebook, and he didn't reply.
Saturday: Eshaan and his mother called the school office on the number printed in the diary. No pending fees, the clerk said. Eshaan showed Siddharth the message on Monday, and they reported it together to the class teacher.

qa.q: How many minutes did the message give to pay by gift card?
qa.a: It gave 30 minutes.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when the message arrived?
qa.a: Eshaan felt a jolt of panic, worried the fees really were late, before the notebook lines helped him slow down.

qa.q: What rule did Eshaan use, and why does it work against most scams?
qa.a: He paused and checked through an official number instead of acting, which beats the rush and secrecy most scams depend on.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the notebook lines now?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel surprised and a bit proud that his dare turned into something useful, and more alert to messages like this himself.

grounding: Shows a teen learning that real institutions do not demand secrecy, instant payment or gift cards, and using a pause to check through an official number.
